prompt: A clean a clock-face geometry figure: a BLUE angle at the centre spanning two rim points A and B, and a RED angle at a third rim point subtending the same A and B. By the inscribed-angle theorem, the blue CENTRAL angle at the centre must be exactly TWICE the red INSCRIBED angle that subtends the same arc A-B. Draw the inscribed (red) angle at exactly half the central (blue) angle. Do NOT make the inscribed angle too large or too small -- the central must be double the inscribed. Plain background, no numbers.
easy_question: This image was supposed to depict a clock-face geometry figure: a BLUE angle at the centre spanning two rim points A and B, and a RED angle at a third rim point subtending the same A and B. reference.q_notext: Ignore the single letters used to label points. Is there any NUMBER, angle value, degree reading or explanatory caption printed anywhere in this picture? Answer yes or no only.

steps.target: point where the two BLUE lines meet each other -- the single spot at the centre of the circle where both blue lines begin and their two ends touch; put the point exactly there, not part-way along either blue line and not where a blue line reaches the circle.

one straight BLUE line -- the whole blue line from one end to the other, boxed so that BOTH of its ends are inside the rectangle: from the spot where the two blue lines meet out to that line's far end on the circle; there are exactly two such blue lines, so box each one on its own and never put both in one rectangle; do not box a red line, the circle's own outline, or a point letter.

point where the two RED lines meet each other -- the single spot on the circle's rim where both red lines begin and their two ends touch; put the point exactly there, not part-way along either red line and not at either place where a red line reaches the far side of the circle.

one straight RED line -- the whole red line from one end to the other, boxed so that BOTH of its ends are inside the rectangle: from the spot where the two red lines meet out to that line's far end on the circle; there are exactly two such red lines, so box each one on its own and never put both in one rectangle; do not box a blue line, the circle's own outline, or a point letter.
